title: What if a gamma-ray burst hit Earth? 💥
subject: space
description:
Would deep-sea life be the only survivor? 👇

A gamma-ray burst within 6,000 light-years could strip up to half of Earth's ozone layer in a 10-second flash, according to University of Kansas and NASA Goddard researchers. Some scientists think one may have triggered the Ordovician extinction 450 million years ago; that idea is a hypothesis, not proven. In October 2022 the brightest burst ever recorded, GRB 221009A, disturbed Earth's ionosphere from 2.4 billion light-years away.

Sources: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio ("Gamma Ray Bursts May Have Caused Ancient Extinctions"), University of Kansas / ScienceDaily (2005), Thomas et al., Astrophysical Journal Letters (2005), NASA HEASARC ("GRB 221009A and the ionosphere"), Northwestern University (2022)

scenes.text: In 10 seconds, Earth could lose half its ozone.
That's a gamma-ray burst within 6,000 light-years, say University of Kansas and NASA Goddard scientists.
Within weeks the ozone layer is cut in half. Recovery takes at least 5 years.
Raw ultraviolet light could kill much of the life on land and in shallow water.
Physicist Brian Thomas thinks one may have caused the Ordovician extinction, 450 million years ago.
In October 2022, a burst 2.4 billion light-years away still jolted our ionosphere.
